title: Houthis Strike Saudi Oil Tankers, Opening Second Front in Red Sea Energy War
excerpt: Iran-aligned Houthis claim missile and drone attacks on two Saudi tankers enforcing a naval blockade, threatening to choke off a critical alternative route for Middle Eastern oil exports to Asia.
body:
• The Houthis launched missile and drone strikes on two Saudi oil tankers, escalating their naval blockade against Saudi Arabia.
  • The attacks occurred shortly after the Houthis declared a full naval blockade on Saudi ports.
  • One tanker, the Encelia, sent a distress call after being hit, but there were no reported casualties or environmental impact.
  • The blockade creates a potential second chokepoint for global oil supplies, alongside Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on Thursday claimed missile and drone strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, marking a dramatic escalation of their naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and raising the spectre of a second chokehold on global oil supplies.

https://x.com/theinformant_x/status/2080082085029843006

The Houthis said they struck the Saudi-flagged tankers Encelia and Layla "for their violation of the blockade decision," according to Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree, who posted the claim on X. The attacks come just days after the group declared a full naval blockade against Saudi Arabian ports on Monday.

Tanker Struck Near Saudi Port

A maritime security source confirmed that the Encelia transmitted a distress call after being struck by a missile near the Saudi port of Jizan late on Wednesday. British maritime risk management group Vanguard said the Saudi-flagged tanker was hit by an unknown projectile on its starboard side approximately 70 nautical miles southwest of Saudi Arabia's Al Shuqaiq, according to Reuters.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations reported a fire on board that the crew was fighting. "There are no reported casualties and no environmental impact," UKMTO said. The attack on the Layla remained unconfirmed as of Thursday.

"The developments represent the first confirmed changes to commercial tanker routing following the embargo and are likely to increase disruption to Saudi crude exports and regional shipping patterns."

— Vanguard, British maritime risk management group

A Coordinated Two-Front Squeeze

The Houthi blockade creates a potential second chokepoint in coordination with Iran's near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the other end of the Arabian Peninsula. Since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28, Saudi Arabia had rerouted millions of barrels per day of crude through its Red Sea port of Yanbu to bypass Hormuz. Saudi crude transiting the Bab el-Mandeb climbed to a record of over four million barrels per day last month, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler.

That alternative route is now under direct threat. Five tankers changed course in the Red Sea on Wednesday alone to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. A day earlier, three tankers — the Xin Long Yang, Rodos, and Amazon — carrying a combined load of Saudi crude bound for China and India made U-turns and headed toward the Suez Canal.

A full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb could cut global oil supply by 7%, according to analysts, sending prices even higher than their current five-week peak. Brent crude jumped nearly 4% to $94.42 a barrel on Wednesday, while WTI crude climbed to $87.45.

Asia and India Bear the Brunt

The disruption hits Asian refiners — particularly India — hardest. The Liberia-flagged tanker Rodos, loaded with Saudi crude at Yanbu and originally headed for India's west coast, was seen signaling the Suez Canal on ship-tracking data via LSEG and Kpler, according to Reuters.

Shipping west through the Suez Canal and around Africa's Cape of Good Hope adds as much as four additional weeks and sharply raises freight and fuel costs compared to the typical eastward route from Yanbu to the Arabian Sea. South Korean refiner Hyundai Oilbank was seeking a Very Large Crude Carrier to load at Yanbu with the option of using the Suez Canal and Egypt's SUMED pipeline.

"Changing behavior by tankers tells us that they are taking the threats seriously," Matt Smith, commodity research director at Kpler, told Reuters. He noted the disruption comes at a particularly difficult time as Saudi crude and products transiting Bab el-Mandeb had climbed to record volumes.

War risk insurance costs for Saudi port calls have already risen, with maritime security company Ambrey advising vessels to "reconsider transiting the Red Sea." Asian refiners' margins for gasoil and jet fuel have soared past $65 a barrel, up from around $20 before the war, according to Reuters.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

India imports roughly 16% of its crude oil from Saudi Arabia, making it one of the kingdom's largest buyers. The rerouting of tankers through the Suez Canal and around Africa will add weeks of delay and billions in additional shipping costs — expenses that will ultimately be passed on to Indian consumers through higher fuel and commodity prices.

For the Indian diaspora, already contending with elevated global inflation driven by the Middle East conflict, the squeeze on oil supply threatens to compound cost-of-living pressures. Remittance values could also be affected as rising energy costs erode household purchasing power in India.

What's Next

The situation remains volatile. A senior Houthi official, Hizam al-Assad, warned on X that attempts to bypass the blockade were "nothing short of utter stupidity" and implied Houthi forces could target Saudi oil-production facilities directly. "The next steps could involve shutting off the tap altogether," he said, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The Saudi-led coalition warned it would respond "firmly" to any threat to its shipping. Meanwhile, the U.S. launched a 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, with Central Command saying the mission would "continue to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten civilian mariners." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi responded: "Our defence doctrine is clear: eye for an eye."

With diplomacy stalled — Trump said the United States has "no interest" in renewed negotiations — the conflict threatens to escalate further, keeping oil prices elevated and shipping routes uncertain for the foreseeable future.
nri_angle: India-bound Saudi crude tankers have been forced to reroute via the Suez Canal, adding weeks to delivery times and raising fuel costs that will ripple through India's economy and the diaspora's cost of living.
author: Diaspora Desk
